children: Predictable government policies and credible institutions could help improve investor confidence in East Africa and boost its prospects of fresh global capital, players in the business community have said.

When governments abruptly shift regulations, introduce policy surprises, or weaken institutional checks, investors lose the ability to calculate risk, which quickly impedes capital inflows into projects.“Capital seeks opportunity, but it also seeks certainty. It seeks returns, but it also seeks stability. It seeks growth, but above all it seeks confidence,” Tanzania businessman and Nation Media Group majority shareholder Rostam Azizi said on Thursday, when he addressed the fourth 200 CEOs Business Forum in Dar es Salaam.

He said competition for global capital had intensified, pushing countries to ensure favourable policy and investment environments for investors seeking expansion and competing for talent.“The question is not whether there is enough capital in the world—of course there is. The question is why that capital should choose East Africa?” Mr Azizi said.

Mshamu Ali Munde, Deputy Minister for Investment in Tanzania, concurred, noting that business confidence heavily draws on predictable policy and sound institutions. “Capital follows opportunity, but it also follows confidence, predictability and credible institutions,” he told the forum while advocating technology and innovation for competitiveness.

The concerns mirror longstanding complaints by business lobbies in the region, who say an increasingly complex and unpredictable regulatory environment is one of the biggest drivers of business costs and, in some cases, forces entrepreneurs to abandon investment projects.

For example, the Kenya Investment Authority (Invest Kenya) recently pointed out that policy predictability is the issue raised most frequently in meetings with prospective investors, reflecting growing concern over abrupt regulatory changes.“Top of mind, the first thing that investors want is predictability,” Invest Kenya CEO John Mwendwa said in an interview with Business Daily in July. “Predictability enables them to plan and model assumptions that resonate with their expectations.”Companies making long-term investments, he said, increasingly want governments to provide stable tax, regulatory and policy environments that allow them to forecast returns with greater certainty.

Data by UNCTAD showed that foreign direct investment inflows to East Africa jumped by 15.38 per cent, to $15 billion in 2025, compared with $13 billion the previous year. “FDI inflows in East Africa were supported by continued investment in large projects and by activity in several LDCs (least developed countries” the UN agency said.

Pius Chaya, Tanzania’s Deputy Minister in the Office of the President in charge of planning and investment, said the government of Tanzania was committed to creating a favourable environment for business and urged corporate organisations to strengthen corporate governance to support their growth beyond the borders.“How do we build more Tanzanian companies that are capable of scaling beyond our borders and remaining strong beyond their founders?” he asked when he delivered remarks at the business forum on behalf of Tanzania’s Prime Minister Mwigulu Nchemba.
